content: The primary treatment for children hospitalized with bronchiolitis is supportive care, which includes oxygen supplementation, respiratory support, and fluid therapy. A significant proportion of infants with bronchiolitis—up to 50%—require non-oral fluid therapy due to dehydration or concerns about the safety of oral feeding. The two main methods of non-oral fluid administration are parenteral (intravenous, IV) and enteral tube feeding (via nasogastric, NG, or orogastric, OG tubes). However, it remains unclear which method is optimal for young children. The objective of this review was to systematically evaluate randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing the effectiveness and safety of parenteral and enteral tube fluid therapy in children under two years of age hospitalized with bronchiolitis. The primary outcome assessed was the difference in the length of hospital stay (in hours) between the two fluid therapy modalities. Secondary outcomes included theoretical length of stay (time when a patient is deemed safe for discharge), time to resume full oral feeding, success of first-attempt fluid modality insertion, need for changes in fluid therapy modality, local complications, parental satisfaction, duration of oxygen supplementation, intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, hospital readmissions, and adverse events. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, including databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as well as conference proceedings and citation lists. Two RCTs involving a total of 810 children met the inclusion criteria. The first trial, conducted by Oakley et al. in Australia and New Zealand, was an open-label, non-blinded RCT involving 759 infants aged 2 to 12 months with bronchiolitis. Participants were randomized to receive either NG tube therapy (381 children) or IV therapy (378 children). The risk of bias was low in most domains. The second trial, conducted by Kugelman et al. in Israel, was also an open-label, non-blinded RCT involving 51 infants under six months of age with moderate bronchiolitis. Of these, 31 infants were assigned to NG or OG tube therapy, and 20 to IV therapy. The risk of bias in this study was unclear in most domains. The findings suggest that enteral tube fluid therapy likely results in little to no difference in the actual length of hospital stay compared to IV fluid therapy (mean difference [MD] 6.8 hours, 95% confidence interval [CI] −4.7 to 18.4 hours; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was little to no difference in the theoretical length of stay (MD 4.4 hours, 95% CI −3.6 to 12.4 hours; moderate-certainty evidence). For secondary outcomes, enteral tube fluid therapy likely results in little to no difference in the time to resume full oral feeding compared to IV fluid therapy (MD 2.8 hours, 95% CI −3.6 to 9.2 hours; moderate-certainty evidence). However, enteral tube therapy likely leads to a significant increase in the success of first-attempt fluid modality insertion (risk ratio [RR] 1.52, 95% CI 1.36 to 1.69; moderate-certainty evidence) and a substantial reduction in the need to change the fluid therapy modality (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.71; moderate-certainty evidence). Local complications were reported less frequently in the enteral tube group compared to the IV group. In the Oakley trial, there were 47 local complications in the IV group versus 30 in the NG tube group. Parental satisfaction was high for both modalities. Enteral tube therapy likely results in little to no difference in the duration of oxygen supplementation (MD 2.2 hours, 95% CI −5.0 to 9.5 hours; moderate-certainty evidence). Compared to IV fluid therapy, enteral tube therapy was associated with a 17% relative reduction in ICU admissions (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.46; moderate-certainty evidence) and a 19% relative reduction in hospital readmissions (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.04; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse events were rare in both groups, with likely little to no difference between the two modalities. In conclusion, based on the two included RCTs, enteral tube fluid therapy likely results in little to no difference in the length of hospital stay compared to IV fluid therapy. However, enteral tube therapy is associated with a higher success rate of first-attempt fluid modality insertion, a lower likelihood of requiring a change in fluid therapy modality, and fewer local complications. Despite bronchiolitis being a common condition in children, the limited number of studies (with fewer than 1,000 participants in total) underscores the need for further multicenter trials. Future research should investigate the type of fluid administered, parent-reported outcomes and preferences, and the role of shared decision-making in the choice of fluid therapy modality.
